body: Founded Fisher & Co. in 1931; author of Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits (1958), whose 15 points (sales growth runway, R&D effectiveness, margins, labour relations, management depth and integrity, long-range outlook) and 'scuttlebutt' method (interview customers, suppliers, competitors and ex-employees) shaped Buffett's shift towards quality growth. Signature trade: bought Motorola in 1955 when it was a car-radio maker and held it until his death in 2004 (folklore-grade; held ~5 decades); also Texas Instruments and Dow Chemical. Track record: never audited or published as a fund series - treat any CAGR claim as unverified. Process: very few holdings, held for decades; sell only if the original analysis was wrong, the company no longer meets the 15 points, or a far better opportunity appears - not because the stock looks expensive. Mistakes he described (Developing an Investment Philosophy): early in his career he tried to time the market and bought weak businesses on cheapness; also, never-sell can mean riding a fading leader (Motorola's long decline after the 1990s). Copyable for Indians: scuttlebutt is very doable - dealer checks, distributor calls, LinkedIn hiring trends, product reviews - and is a genuine individual edge in small/mid caps under-covered by analysts.
title: Philip Fisher - scuttlebutt growth investing
